c.tagline: Baroque bastions guard a golden harbour capital.

taxi.fareNote: Licensed Malta taxis (white, roof-signed) run on meters within urban areas; airport transfers and pre-booked rides typically use fixed, pre-agreed rates instead.

emergency.note: 112 is the EU-wide single emergency number covering police, ambulance and fire across Malta; it is free and works from any phone.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Valletta itself is calm; watch pickpockets in sightseeing crowds and save nightlife caution for nearby Paceville's rowdy bars.

hood_desc: Malta's compact, UNESCO-listed walled capital packed with baroque churches, palaces and rooftop bars; ideal for first-time visitors who want to be steps from the main sights.
A lively seafront town across the harbour with a long promenade, shopping and ferry links to Valletta; suited to travelers wanting modern comforts and easy transit.
Malta's main nightlife, casino and dining hub around Spinola Bay, mixing business hotels with clubs; best for younger travelers who want bars within walking distance.
The hilltop 'Silent City' of Mdina and its quieter neighbor Rabat, full of medieval streets and catacombs; perfect for travelers seeking a tranquil, atmospheric base.
A north-coast resort strip with budget-friendly hotels, promenades and dive schools; suits families and value-focused travelers who don't mind busing into Valletta.

water.note: Desalinated tap water meets EU standards and is safe from the kitchen tap, though bathroom taps (fed by storage tanks) are best avoided for drinking.

transit.pay: Most riders buy a rechargeable tallinja card (cheaper per-ride rate) online or at kiosks, or tap a contactless bank card directly on the bus reader; single paper tickets can also be bought in cash from the driver at a higher price. Ferries are paid for with cash or card at the kiosk/turnstile per crossing.
transit.hours: Buses run roughly 5am-11pm on most routes, with limited weekend Night Route (N-series) service; the Valletta-Sliema and Valletta-Three Cities ferries run roughly 6:45am-11pm depending on season.
transit.note: Malta has no metro, tram or rail; the island-wide 'tallinja' bus network run by Malta Public Transport is the backbone of public transit, supplemented by short harbour ferry hops in and out of Valletta.

transit.m: X4 direct express bus to Valletta (~30-40 min)
Night bus / other X-series routes to harbour towns

tip.r: Tipping is not mandatory; rounding up taxi fares and leaving 5-10% in restaurants when service isn't already included is appreciated.

food.name: Pastizzi
food.desc: Diamond-shaped flaky pastries filled with ricotta or mushy peas, eaten hot from paper for small change. Malta's national snack.

places.name: Nenu the Artisan Baker
places.note: Bakery-restaurant in the capital doing traditional ricotta and pea pastizzi.

places.name: Cafe Jubilee
places.note: Cosy vintage cafe-bar open late, good for pastizzi with a coffee or beer.

places.name: Is-Serkin Crystal Palace
places.note: The island's most famous pastizzeria since 1945; worth the trip out to Mdina.

food.name: Fenkata (rabbit stew)
food.desc: Rabbit slow-cooked in red wine, garlic and bay, traditionally eaten as a long shared feast with the pasta course served first.

places.name: Nenu the Artisan Baker
places.note: Hearty stew with plenty of meat, potatoes and grilled vegetables.

places.name: Palazzo Preca
places.note: Sister chefs cooking a refined rabbit dish in a vaulted 16th-century palazzo.

places.name: Legligin
places.note: Basement wine bar serving a tasting menu of Maltese dishes; book ahead.

food.name: Ftira
food.desc: Ring-shaped sourdough flatbread rubbed with tomato and filled with tuna, capers, olives, onion and Maltese oil. UNESCO-listed craft.

places.name: Nenu the Artisan Baker

places.name: Is-Suq tal-Belt
places.note: Restored covered market with food stalls, an easy stop for a quick local lunch.

places.name: Cafe Jubilee
places.note: Reliable ftira and other Maltese snacks served from morning until late.

food.name: Bragioli
food.desc: Beef olives: thin slices of beef rolled around minced meat, egg, herbs and breadcrumbs, then braised slowly in red wine and tomato.

places.name: Legligin
places.note: Local ingredients and Maltese wine in a stone-vaulted cellar setting.

places.name: Beati Paoli
places.note: Traditional Maltese kitchen near the Grand Harbour, strong on braised meats.

places.name: Palazzo Preca
places.note: Polished versions of the island's home-cooking classics; reservations advised.

food.name: Lampuki pie
food.desc: Autumn pie of lampuki (dorado) baked with spinach, olives, capers and walnuts under pastry. Only around when the fish are running.

places.name: Rubino
places.note: Valletta institution since 1906 with a daily-changing traditional menu.

places.name: Legligin
places.note: Puts lampuki on the menu in season, matched with Maltese wines.

places.name: Beati Paoli
places.note: Fresh local fish and classic Maltese recipes made to order.

food.name: Timpana
food.desc: Baked macaroni with beef and pork ragu, egg and cheese, encased in pastry and cut into thick slabs. Maltese comfort food at its heaviest.

places.name: Nenu the Artisan Baker
places.note: Wood-oven bakes of the island's staple pasta dishes in a converted bakery.

places.name: The Maltese Kitchen
places.note: Casual spot with big portions of timpana, minestra and other homely plates.

places.name: Rubino
places.note: Family-run dining room known for old recipes and its imqaret and cassata.

food.name: Kinnie
food.desc: Malta's bittersweet amber soft drink made from bitter oranges and aromatic herbs, invented in 1952. Served very cold, often with a slice of orange.

places.name: Is-Suq tal-Belt
places.note: Food-hall counters pour it ice cold; good with a plate of pastizzi.

places.name: Cafe Jubilee
places.note: Also mixes Kinnie with local spirits if you want it long and cold.

places.name: Nenu the Artisan Baker
places.note: Classic pairing of Kinnie with ftira or pastizzi in a traditional setting.

food.name: Cisk lager
food.desc: Malta's own pale lager, brewed since 1928 and the default beer across the islands. Best drunk cold in the harbour breeze.

places.name: Bridge Bar
places.note: Steps and cushions on a stone staircase, with live jazz on summer Fridays.

places.name: The Pub
places.note: Tiny historic pub known for its Oliver Reed connection; standing room only.

places.name: Cafe Jubilee

landmarks: St. John's Co-Cathedral
Behind a plain baroque facade lies an astonishingly opulent interior of gilded carvings and Caravaggio's masterpiece 'The Beheading of Saint John the Baptist.'
Upper Barrakka Gardens
Perched on the bastions above the Grand Harbour, these elegant gardens deliver Valletta's most photographed panorama, especially during the daily noon cannon salute.
Grand Harbour
One of the world's finest natural deep-water harbors, its honey-colored fortified walls and bastions create an unforgettable maritime backdrop for the capital.
Fort St. Elmo
This star-shaped 16th-century fortress guarding the harbor entrance withstood the brutal Great Siege of 1565 and now houses Malta's National War Museum.
Grandmaster's Palace
This former residence of the Knights of St. John, now Malta's presidential palace, showcases opulent state rooms, historic armories, and frescoed corridors.
Valletta Skyline from the Three Cities
Viewed across the Grand Harbour, Valletta's honey-hued domes, spires, and fortifications form one of the Mediterranean's most iconic and photographed cityscapes.
Auberge de Castille
The most magnificent of the Knights' auberges, this baroque palace with its grand staircase and ornate facade now serves as the Prime Minister's office.
Triton Fountain
Three bronze Tritons hoisting a giant basin greet visitors at Valletta's City Gate entrance, making this dramatic fountain an unmissable arrival landmark.
Saluting Battery
This historic gun battery beneath the Upper Barrakka Gardens fires ceremonial cannon salutes daily, echoing centuries of naval tradition over the Grand Harbour.
Republic Street
Valletta's pedestrianized main artery runs the length of the city, lined with historic churches, palaces, boutiques, and cafes perfect for leisurely exploring.

train.note: Malta has no railway at all — the island's old Valletta–Mdina line closed in 1931. Get around by Malta Public Transport bus or, for Sicily and beyond, by ferry or air.

bus.note: Malta is an island with no international coach routes. Malta Public Transport (tallinja) runs the island-wide bus network from the main terminus just outside Valletta's City Gate — see https://www.publictransport.com.mt/ for routes and tickets.

ferry.note: Virtu Ferries' high-speed catamaran crosses to Pozzallo in about 1h45 and runs year-round (more sailings in summer), departing from the sea passenger terminal in Valletta's Grand Harbour — bring your passport/ID. Ponte Ferries' rival Malta–Augusta service ceased in 2023 and GNV carries no Malta passengers. The domestic Gozo Channel ferry (https://www.gozochannel.com/) leaves from Ċirkewwa in the island's north, not Valletta; Valletta Ferry Services runs short harbour boats to Sliema and the Three Cities.

half.name: Mdina
half.blurb: Silent walled medieval city of golden stone, palaces and bastion views across the island.

half.name: Gozo
half.blurb: Greener sister island of rugged cliffs, ancient temples, salt pans and quiet fishing villages.

half.name: Comino Blue Lagoon
half.blurb: Tiny island's turquoise lagoon with dazzling clear water perfect for swimming and snorkeling.

half.name: Marsaxlokk
half.blurb: Colorful fishing village where painted luzzu boats bob beside a lively Sunday seafood market.

half.name: Blue Grotto
half.blurb: Sea caves and arches glowing electric blue, best explored by small boat tour.

half.name: Hagar Qim & Mnajdra Temples
half.blurb: Megalithic temples older than the pyramids, standing on cliffs above the sparkling sea.
